_doc.purpose: How held living stock changes each year (sim/world/stock_dynamics.py, sim/living_stock/yearly.py). A material listed here is multiplied by its natural increase when the holding is at least its breeding minimum, and lowered by its annual loss; both are fractions of the holding, applied as expected values (no dice).
_doc.fields: walks: true for animals that are driven to market on foot (the drove mode); other stock (seed, cuttings, eggs) is carried as goods. natural_increase: fraction of the holding added in a year by breeding or propagation. annual_loss: fraction lost in a year to death, spoilage or failed sets. breeding_minimum_units: smallest holding that can breed (a breeding group, a viable planting), in the material's unit; below it nothing is added. basis: how the rates were reached. source: author or body, title and year of what the figures came from. confidence: A, B or C, the grade of that source (A a handbook or measured, C a web summary or estimate). grows_on: what limits the holding's yearly gain: pasture (the grass of the stock's place, sim/geography/food_pasture.py, and the live weight already grazing there) or arable (the arable land of the place at the output per hectare of the stock's production entry); absent means unlimited. species: the herd animal ids (data/world/geography/resources/animals.json) the stock is kept from; the held lot also loses the endemic disease loss of its place for the hardiest of them (data/disease/endemic/), and a lot whose loss outruns its natural increase dies out. The labour of any gain is the labour of that production entry, bought at the going wage; a purse that cannot pay buys less gain.
_doc.status: Every rate here is a TEMPORARY HEURISTIC unless the row carries a source: a stated order-of-magnitude estimate from the reasoning in its basis. The gain of a row with grows_on is limited by the pasture or arable land of the place and paid in labour; a row without it is not.

draught_animal_kg.basis: TEMPORARY HEURISTIC, live weight of working cattle and horses. About half a herd is breeding females and a female calves or foals in about six years in ten, so 0.3 young per head per year; about a third of the young die or are culled before work age, leaving about 0.2. Adult mortality of a few percent a year (disease, accident, murrain) is taken as 0.05. A breeding group is a male and three females, about four animals of about 300 kg live weight, so 1200 kg. Estimates, not checked against a source.

ramie_stock_kg.basis: TEMPORARY HEURISTIC, rhizome cuttings. Ramie spreads by rhizome and is propagated by dividing it; a stand can be divided into several times its planting weight in a year, but cuttings are held as stock here and not planted out, so only a modest 0.3 is taken for the part divided and replanted in a nursery. Rot and failed sets lose about a tenth of stored cuttings a year. A viable nursery is taken as a few kilograms of cuttings. Estimates, not checked against a source.

silkworm_eggs_kg.basis: TEMPORARY HEURISTIC, eggs of the silkworm. A held lot does not multiply: eggs become more eggs only by being hatched, reared on mulberry leaf to cocoons and the moths allowed to lay, which is the production entry silkworm_eggs_kg, not a rate of the lot. Eggs are stored cool and hatch the following spring; a lot kept past one season loses most of its viability, so half of a held lot is taken as lost in a year. Estimates, not checked against a source.

cashmere_goat_kg.basis: TEMPORARY HEURISTIC, live weight of fine-undercoat goats. Does kid about once a year with some twins, about one kid per doe and about half the flock are does, so 0.5 kids per head; about a third of kids die before their first winter, leaving about 0.3. Adult mortality is taken as 0.08. A breeding flock is a buck and four does, about five animals of about 30 kg, so 150 kg. Estimates, not checked against a source.

angora_goat_kg.basis: TEMPORARY HEURISTIC, live weight of Angora goats. The same reasoning and numbers as cashmere_goat_kg: about one kid per doe, half the flock does, a third of kids lost, adult mortality 0.08, a breeding flock of five animals of about 30 kg. Estimates, not checked against a source.

jute_seed_kg.basis: TEMPORARY HEURISTIC, jute seed. Seed multiplies only by being sown and harvested, which is the production entry jute_seed_kg, not a rate of held seed. Stored seed loses viability to damp, insects and age; about three tenths of a held lot is taken as unusable after a year. Estimates, not checked against a source.

hop_rhizome_kg.basis: TEMPORARY HEURISTIC, hop rhizome cuttings. The hop is a perennial that is propagated by cuttings from the rootstock; a nursery of cuttings multiplies by about a third a year when divided and replanted. About a tenth of held cuttings dry out or rot. A viable planting is taken as a couple of kilograms of cuttings. Estimates, not checked against a source.

pyrethrum_stock_kg.basis: TEMPORARY HEURISTIC, pyrethrum planting stock (crowns and seed). The perennial is propagated by dividing crowns; the same modest 0.3 increase and 0.1 loss as hop_rhizome_kg, with a viable planting of a couple of kilograms. Estimates, not checked against a source.

dairy_cattle_kg.source: FAO, 'Production parameters of ruminants in traditional systems' (chapter 5 of the FAO review of ruminant production in sub-Saharan Africa; fao.org/4/Y4176E/y4176e08.htm; undated, 1990s): calving rate 58.7 percent, calf mortality 21.7 percent, adult cow mortality 6.3 percent, age at first calving about 48 months, milk offtake about 250 kg per lactation.
dairy_cattle_kg.basis: Live weight of milk cattle. Half a herd is breeding cows, calving 0.587 a year, and 21.7 percent of calves die, so 0.5 x 0.587 x (1 - 0.217) per head. Loss is the sourced adult mortality. The first calf comes after about four years, so the rate is a steady-state herd figure and a freshly founded herd breeds slower (not modelled). Yield: about 250 kg of milk offtake per cow per lactation in the same systems. The breeding minimum, a bull and three cows, is a TEMPORARY HEURISTIC; the animal weight behind it is not sourced.

pepper_vine_stock_kg.source: Tamil Nadu Agricultural University, Agritech Portal, 'Horticulture: Spice Crops: Pepper' (agritech.tnau.ac.in/horticulture/horti_spice crops_pepper.html; undated): about 60 cuttings per mother vine per year by the serpentine method, 80 to 85 percent rooting by the trench method, first bearing in the third or fourth year, 2 to 3 kg of dry pepper per vine per year.
pepper_vine_stock_kg.basis: Kilograms of rooted vine cuttings and young vines. Sourced ceiling: 60 cuttings per mother vine at 80 percent rooting, so tens of rooted vines per mother a year; loss is the failed set share, 1 - 0.8. The increase is still capped at a doubling a year, a TEMPORARY HEURISTIC, although the yearly growth is now held by the stock's arable land and its labour is bought (sim/living_stock/rules.py): the sourced propagation figures are counts of cuttings or seeds per plant, and no source was found for what a cutting weighs against its mother plant, so a count cannot be turned into a ratio of kilograms; the cap stands for that mass ratio until one is sourced. Years to first yield: three to four. Yield per vine: 2 to 3 kg of dry pepper. A viable planting of a few kilograms is a TEMPORARY HEURISTIC.

tea_plant_stock_kg.source: Clonal propagation of tea (Krishi Vigyan Kendra Mokokchung leaflet; kvkmokokchung.in; undated, as summarised by search): 50 to 300 healthy cuttings per mother bush per year; University of Hawaii CTAHR, 'In-Tray Procedure for Rooting Tea Cuttings' (SCM-35): cutting survival 97 percent in one year and 86 percent in another; tea-industry yield classes of 2000 to 4000 kg of made tea per hectare.
tea_plant_stock_kg.basis: Kilograms of rooted tea cuttings. Sourced ceiling: 50 to 300 cuttings per mother bush a year; loss is the failed share, about 1 - 0.9 from the 86 to 97 percent survival. The increase is still capped at a doubling a year, a TEMPORARY HEURISTIC, although the yearly growth is now held by the stock's arable land and its labour is bought (sim/living_stock/rules.py): the sourced propagation figures are counts of cuttings or seeds per plant, and no source was found for what a cutting weighs against its mother plant, so a count cannot be turned into a ratio of kilograms; the cap stands for that mass ratio until one is sourced. Mother bushes are usable after five to six years; first plucking about three to four years after planting out. Yield: 2000 to 4000 kg of made tea per hectare in established fields. The tea-industry yield classes are from a web summary and were not checked in the primary text.

coffee_seedling_kg.source: Agriculture Institute, 'Coffee Propagation Methods: Seed and Vegetative Techniques' (agriculture.institute; undated): nursery loss of 20 to 30 percent to damping-off, temperature and moisture, 6 to 9 months in the nursery, first yield 3 to 4 years from seed; smallholder green-bean yields of 500 to 1000 kg per hectare per year (a coffee-sustainability review, Expl Agric 2005, vol 41, pp 449-473, as summarised by search).
coffee_seedling_kg.basis: Kilograms of coffee seedlings. Loss is the midpoint of the 20 to 30 percent nursery loss, rounded up for field setting. Coffee is raised from seed, a tree bears many seeds, so the propagation ceiling is far above a doubling. The increase is still capped at a doubling a year, a TEMPORARY HEURISTIC, although the yearly growth is now held by the stock's arable land and its labour is bought (sim/living_stock/rules.py): the sourced propagation figures are counts of cuttings or seeds per plant, and no source was found for what a cutting weighs against its mother plant, so a count cannot be turned into a ratio of kilograms; the cap stands for that mass ratio until one is sourced. Years to first yield: three to four. Yield: about 2 to 4 kg of cherry per mature tree, 400 to 800 g of green coffee. Web-summary sources, not handbooks; grade C.

sugar_cane_sett_kg.source: Cane Advisory Services (caneadvisory.ac.in, 'Seed Rate'; undated): 42,000 to 45,000 three-bud setts, 50 to 60 quintals, plant a hectare; a sugarcane planting-techniques review reports a conventional multiplication of about 11 to 12 against 100 to 150 from tissue culture; two-bud setts germinate about 65 to 70 percent (sugarcane agronomy lab manual, mcconline.org.in).
sugar_cane_sett_kg.basis: Kilograms of seed cane (setts). Sourced multiplication: a seed nursery hectare plants about 11 to 12 hectares by conventional multiplication, the same planting rate per hectare in each, so a lot of setts multiplies about eleven-fold in a year (an increase of 10); loss is the failed share, 1 - 0.7 from germination of about 65 to 70 percent. The increase is not capped: the yearly growth is held by the arable land of the stock's place at the nursery output per hectare of the production entry, and its labour is bought at the going wage (sim/living_stock/rules.py). Seed cane per hectare planted: 5000 to 6000 kg. Years to first yield: about one year (a plant cane crop). A planting is not a source of seed after the ratoon crop, which carries disease.

rubber_planting_stock_kg.source: Warren Dean, 'Brazil and the Struggle for Rubber' (Cambridge University Press, 1987) for the 1876 transfer of Hevea seed from the Amazon to Kew and then to Ceylon and Singapore; Sethuraj and Mathew (eds), 'Natural Rubber: Biology, Cultivation and Technology' (Elsevier, 1992) for nursery, budding and tapping practice. Both are named from memory and were not opened in this session; no figure below was checked against their text.
rubber_planting_stock_kg.basis: Kilograms of budded stumps and seedlings of the rubber tree. TEMPORARY HEURISTIC, unsourced figures: a budded-stump nursery is taken to double its stock a year (a budwood garden of selected clones gives buds for several stumps each, but what a stump weighs against its mother tree is not known to me, so the doubling stands for that ratio until it is sourced), and about a fifth of stumps are lost in lifting, transport and the first season in the field. A viable planting is taken as a few kilograms. The yearly gain is held by the arable land of the stock's place and its labour is bought (sim/living_stock/rules.py). Years to first tapping: about six to seven for a stump planted out (docs/knowledge/76_farming_food_deep.md, ag2_rubber_plantation, confidence C).

potato_seed_tuber_kg.basis: Seed tubers of the potato. A tuber multiplies only by being planted and lifted, which is the production entry, not a rate of the held lot. SOURCED (read): an Andean organic plot sowed about 1850 kg of seed per hectare and lifted 7.34 kg per kg sown (Quispe Condori and Pari Choquechambi 2025, doi 10.25127/agrops.20252.1087, pp. 6-9; one experimental plot). TEMPORARY HEURISTIC, unsourced: half of a held lot lost in a year, since a stored tuber sprouts, rots or shrivels within a season or two without cool dark storage.

maize_seed_kg.basis: Maize grain kept for sowing. Seed multiplies only by being sown and harvested, which is the production entry, not a rate of the held lot. SOURCED (read): milpa sowing is two to three seeds per hill, hills 80 by 40 cm, about 62500 plants per hectare (Cuanalo-de la Cerda and Uicab-Covoh 2006, Terra Latinoamericana 24(3):401-408, p. 404); the seed mass per hectare is not stated. TEMPORARY HEURISTIC, unsourced: about a fifth of a held lot unusable after a year, since dry grain keeps viability a few years if kept dry and free of weevil.

cacao_seed_kg.basis: Cacao beans kept for planting. Multiplication is by planting and a bearing tree, which is the production entry, not a rate of the held lot. SOURCED (read): trees become productive two to four years after planting (Daymond et al., Global Review of Cocoa Farming Systems, University of Reading for ICCO, section 2.4). TEMPORARY HEURISTIC, unsourced: nearly all of a held lot lost within a year, since the seed is recalcitrant, does not survive drying and loses viability within weeks unless planted out in a nursery; no source opened for the loss rate.

sheep_kg.dung_and_fodder_source: Dung and fodder per head, by the species row. Fresh excreta as a share of live weight a day: USDA NRCS, Agricultural Waste Management Field Handbook, Part 651, chapter 4 'Agricultural Waste Characteristics' (rev. July 1996; opened as a PDF): Table 4-18, lamb waste as excreted, weight 40.00 lb/d/1000#, so 0.04 for sheep; Table 4-8, beef waste as excreted, cow 63.00 lb/d/1000# (feeder yearlings 51.20 to 59.10), so 0.063 for cattle. The chapter has no goat row: goats use the sheep figure (no source found for goats; TEMPORARY HEURISTIC). Collected share is the part of the day in a fold, byre or night corral, a third (assumed): dung dropped at pasture is not gathered. Winter ration: dry matter intake of two percent of live weight a day (South Australian government fact sheet 'Calculating dry matter intakes for various classes of stock', Managing livestock in dry times, opened as a PDF: 'Animal on dry pasture or poor quality feed: 2%'; 'Cattle and sheep generally consume between 2-3% of their live weight in DM daily') over ninety days of stall or fold feeding (assumed), half of it straw at ninety percent dry matter (assumed). Bran is a supplement for milked animals (assumed). Confidence D: the excreta share and the dry matter intake are read (above); the collected share, winter days and straw share are assumed. Husbandry assumptions, searched in the same pass: the dung collected from an animal is the share of its day spent in the fold or byre (an extension worksheet, Keeping Track of Manure Nutrients in Dairy Pastures, https://www.kpu.ca/sites/default/files/Keeping%20Track%20of%20Manure%20Nutrients%20in%20Dairy%20Pastures.pdf, opened: a cow grazed 9 hours by day and 9 by night 'deposits 75 percent of her daily waste production' in the field and the other 25 percent in the confinement facility), so the collected share of a third is 8 hours of 24 in a night fold, the same order as that example's 25 percent. Winter housing: a Romanian dairy study (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3674972, opened) has cows pasturing 182 days a year, so about half a year indoors in a continental climate; the 90 days of stall or fold feeding here are a milder Mediterranean-and-oceanic ballpark under that. No page gave a straw share of a winter ration or a draught share of offtake; those stay assumed.
sheep_kg.source: McKinnon and Rocha, 'Reproduction, mortality and growth of indigenous sheep and goats in Mozambique' (FAO, fao.org/4/x5464b/x5464b0w.htm; opened): 79.1 percent of ewes and 91.9 percent of does gave birth in a year, deaths from birth to eight months about 20 percent, whole-flock mortality 16 and 15 percent; litter 1.03 lambs per lambing in an Ethiopian smallholder study (as summarised by a search, not opened). Offtake 20.8 percent a year for sheep (mean of reported traditional-system rates) and mature live weight 28.7 kg ewes, 31.2 kg rams: FAO, 'Production parameters of ruminants in traditional systems', fao.org/4/Y4176E/y4176e08.htm, opened. Dressing percentage: Montana State University Extension (Sanders County), 'Dressing percentage' note, montana.edu/extension/sanders/understanding%20the%20dressing%20percenage.pdf, opened as a PDF: 'For lambs, the normal range is 44 to 56% with an average of 54 for shorn lambs and 52 for unshorn lambs. For calculations, 50% is often used.' The rest (live weight, fleece, fat and hide shares, salt lick, stocking rate): no source found; kept as labelled heuristics (Complaints/646). Fleece and hide, read in the Complaints/532 and 670 source pass: Wilson, 'Small ruminant production and the small ruminant genetic resource in tropical Africa' (FAO), fao.org/4/t0376e/t0376e09.htm (opened), Ethiopian Highland (Menz) sheep, traditional sector: 'WOOL. Yield : 400-1000 g per clip, usually 2 clips per year', so 0.8 to 2.0 kg a head-year; 1.0 kg lies in that range (a hair-and-wool highland sheep, a bracket and not a Mediterranean measurement). FAO, 'Manual for the slaughter of small ruminants in developing countries' (Animal Production and Health Paper 49), section 10.2, fao.org/4/x6552e/x6552e10.htm, opened: the approximate yield of green hides and skins in pastoral tropical livestock, as a percentage of live weight: cattle 6 to 8 (average 18 kg), large sheep and goats 14 to 16 (6 kg), dwarf sheep and goats 10 to 12 (4 kg). The 30 kg unimproved sheep is taken in the dwarf class, midpoint 11 percent (was 8, no source). Salt, read in the Complaint 670 pass: New Mexico State University sheep nutrition page (https://aces-newmexicosheep.nmsu.edu/nutrition/requirements.html, opened): 'supplemental salt should be provided to range ewes at a level of 8 to 11 g of salt per head per day'; midpoint 9.5 g x 365 = 3.47 kg, taken as 3.5 (was 4.0, no source); Merck Veterinary Manual (merckvetmanual.com, nutrition-sheep, opened): 'Mature sheep will consume approximately 9 g ... of salt daily'. Goats: the sheep figure scaled by live weight, 9.5 g x 25/30 x 365 = 2.9 kg (was 3.0). Cattle: Agriorbit, 'The low-down on salt intake' (https://agriorbit.com/?p=245351, opened): 'Mature cows require approximately 30g of salt ... daily', 30 g x 365 = 10.95 kg, the row's 11 kg. Stocking, read in the same pass: Sange et al., LRRD 30(5) 2018 (https://lrrd.org/lrrd30/5/sange30079.html, opened): semi-arid carrying capacity 'around 3 TLU (ha/LU/yr)' with upland and midland sites at 2 to 4 ha per tropical livestock unit, Pratt and Gwynne's 4 ha, and a table note that 'one cow equals four goats or sheep'; so cattle at 0.5 head a hectare (2 ha each) is the better-watered end, and 4 sheep or goats a cow gives 2 a hectare, the goat row, with sheep at 1.5 inside 1.3 (3 ha a cow) to 2. Goats: a Greek kermes-oak study tested 1, 2 and 4 goats a hectare a year (https://agris.fao.org/search/es/records/64775fb1a3fd11e4303b9c4c, opened abstract), with only the 4 a hectare rate significantly degrading vegetation and gain, so 2 is a sustainable rate there. Fat share, read in the Complaint 670 pass: USDA AMS By-Product Drop Value Report - Cow (https://www.ams.usda.gov/mnreports/ams_2834.pdf, opened as a PDF): renderable tallow yield 3.68 lb per 100 lb live weight of a typical slaughter cow, 3.68 percent of live weight; fat share of the carcass is that over the dressing fraction: cattle 0.0368 / 0.442 = 0.083, sheep 0.0368 / 0.5 = 0.074, goats 0.0368 / 0.45 = 0.082 (the cow's yield applied to the small ruminants by analogy; a modern slaughter cow is fatter than a traditional animal). Complaint 532 pass: McKinnon and Rocha (the same page, fao.org/4/x5464b/x5464b0w.htm, re-opened): Table 1 litter size 1.36 for Nguni sheep (269 births, 366 young) and 1.62 for Landim goats (239 births, 388 young), which replace the unopened 1.03 above. Breeding-ewe share of the flock: PMC5963035 (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5963035, opened), South Wollo, Ethiopia, Table 1: 29.2 percent overall, 27.1 and 25.5 percent in the two F1-cross strata and 36.5 percent in the indigenous Wollo highland stratum; the indigenous stratum is the unimproved analogue, so 0.365 replaces the assumed 0.6 (and the net increase 0.314 less loss 0.08 = 0.234 still covers the 0.208 offtake). Complaint 532 pass 4, labour: shearing by hand blades, commercial blade shearers shear 140 sheep in an 8-hour day (Wikipedia, Blade shearing, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blade_shearing, opened), 3.4 minutes or 0.057 hour a sheep (was 0.4 hour, no source). Slaughter, flaying and jointing 3 hours a carcass: a practiced hand can kill, skin and gut a 100 to 300 lb animal in under an hour (20 to 30 minutes estimated) and a first-timer should allow 3 to 4 hours for the full session (a forum thread, https://permies.com/mobile/t/96973/TIME-animal-species-killing-butchering, opened), so 3 hours is the full session of an unpractised butcher; a home pig slaughter by two people took about 4 hours a pig each (Grit, https://www.grit.com/animals/livestock/pigs/first-pig-slaughter/, opened). Winter straw share of the ration 0.5: dry fodder gives 13 percent of feed dry matter from August to October and 52 percent from January to April on southern Indian mixed farms (R. E. McDowell, FAO, https://www.fao.org/4/x5495e/x5495e02.htm, opened), so 0.5 holds in the winter months. Adult loss 0.08: between 1.6 percent for adult sheep and 16 percent for the whole flock (McKinnon and Rocha, see above). Dung gathering 3 hours a tonne: bracket, upper only: mucking out a stable thoroughly takes 15 to 20 minutes (Just Horse Riders, https://justhorseriders.co.uk/blogs/news/efficiency-in-equine-care-how-long-does-it-take-to-muck-out-a-stable, opened) for the 25 kg a day of a 400 kg horse's dung (0.063 x 400, NRCS above), 9.9 to 13 hours a tonne including bedding and urine, so dung alone, gathered from a fold, is at or below that; no lower figure was opened.
sheep_kg.basis: Live weight of sheep of an unimproved breed, in kilograms. Increase = 0.365 of the flock breeding ewes (Wollo highland indigenous sheep, Table 1 of Tesfa et al. below) x 0.791 lambing x 1.36 lambs a lambing (Nguni sheep, McKinnon and Rocha Table 1) x 0.8 surviving to eight months = 0.314. Loss 0.08 of the flock is adult mortality (assumed: about half the whole-flock mortality sourced above). A breeding group is five animals of about 35 kg, 175 kg (TEMPORARY HEURISTIC). Herd parameters beside it feed the herd recipe in data/production/95_herds.json: 1.5 head per hectare of rough Mediterranean grazing (the stocking rate the earlier wool entry used, an estimate), a 30 kg mean live weight at slaughter (lambs and culls mixed), a clip of 1 kg greasy wool a head (inside the 0.8 to 2.0 kg a year read for Menz sheep; see source), mutton fat trimmed for rendering 8 percent of the carcass, a raw skin 11 percent of live weight (FAO dwarf class, see source), 4 kg of salt a head-year (about 10 g a day; no source found). Offtake 0.208 is below natural increase less loss (0.31), so the herd is sustained.

goat_kg.dung_and_fodder_source: Dung and fodder per head, by the species row. Fresh excreta as a share of live weight a day: USDA NRCS, Agricultural Waste Management Field Handbook, Part 651, chapter 4 'Agricultural Waste Characteristics' (rev. Bran is a supplement for milked animals (assumed). Confidence D: the excreta share and the dry matter intake are read (above); the collected share, winter days and straw share are assumed. Husbandry assumptions, searched in the same pass: the dung collected from an animal is the share of its day spent in the fold or byre (an extension worksheet, Keeping Track of Manure Nutrients in Dairy Pastures, https://www.kpu.ca/sites/default/files/Keeping%20Track%20of%20Manure%20Nutrients%20in%20Dairy%20Pastures.pdf, opened: a cow grazed 9 hours by day and 9 by night 'deposits 75 percent of her daily waste production' in the field and the other 25 percent in the confinement facility), so the collected share of a third is 8 hours of 24 in a night fold, the same order as that example's 25 percent. No page gave a straw share of a winter ration or a draught share of offtake; those stay assumed. Goat excreta share: no opened page gave goat faeces against live weight (an extension goat handbook line of 2 to 6 percent of live weight in fresh faeces appeared in a search summary only, not opened); the sheep figure stays. Goat excreta bracket: see the cattle row's source.
goat_kg.source: McKinnon and Rocha, 'Reproduction, mortality and growth of indigenous sheep and goats in Mozambique' (FAO, fao.org/4/x5464b/x5464b0w.htm; opened): 79.1 percent of ewes and 91.9 percent of does gave birth in a year, deaths from birth to eight months about 20 percent, whole-flock mortality 16 and 15 percent; offtake 21.4 percent a year for goats (mean of reported traditional-system rates) and mature live weight 27.8 kg does, 32.0 kg bucks: FAO, 'Production parameters of ruminants in traditional systems', fao.org/4/Y4176E/y4176e08.htm, opened. Dressing percentage: Montana State University Extension (Sanders County), 'Dressing percentage' note, opened as a PDF: 'For goats, dressing percentage varies from 40% in very young animals to 56% in entire mature males. 45% is a good average to use.' Okello, 'A survey of the productivity and functions of goats in Uganda', fao.org/4/x5464b/x5464b16.htm, opened, Tables 1-3: dressed carcass weight of Small East African, Mubende and Kigezi goats runs 44.1 to 58.3 percent by sex, age and region, so 45 is at the low end of that survey (kept, the extension average). The rest (litter, live weight, milk per lactation, horn, salt lick, stocking rate) : no source found; kept as labelled heuristics (Complaints/646). Milk and hide, read in the Complaints/532 and 670 source pass: Wilson, 'Small ruminant production and the small ruminant genetic resource in tropical Africa' (FAO), fao.org/4/t0376e/t0376e06.htm (opened), Tswana goat under the traditional system: 'MILK. Lactation length: up to and in excess of 180 days in traditional system. Yield: 284 g/d in addition to that taken by kids'; 284 g x 180 days = 51.12 kg a lactation, and half the herd are milked does (assumed), so 25.56 kg a head-year (was 50, from an unsourced 100 kg a lactation). Litter 1.37 (n=285) and 95 percent of 298 breeding females kidding in the traditional system are in the same entry; the row's 1.1 kids a doe is left as assumed because changing the increase moves the herd-growth entries. FAO, 'Manual for the slaughter of small ruminants in developing countries' (Animal Production and Health Paper 49), section 10.2, fao.org/4/x6552e/x6552e10.htm, opened: the approximate yield of green hides and skins in pastoral tropical livestock, as a percentage of live weight: cattle 6 to 8 (average 18 kg), large sheep and goats 14 to 16 (6 kg), dwarf sheep and goats 10 to 12 (4 kg). Goats of 25 kg are taken in the dwarf class, midpoint 11 percent (was 8, no source). Salt and stocking: see the sheep row's source (Complaint 670 pass). Fat share, read in the Complaint 670 pass: USDA AMS By-Product Drop Value Report - Cow (https://www.ams.usda.gov/mnreports/ams_2834.pdf, opened as a PDF): renderable tallow yield 3.68 lb per 100 lb live weight of a typical slaughter cow, 3.68 percent of live weight; fat share of the carcass is that over the dressing fraction: cattle 0.0368 / 0.442 = 0.083, sheep 0.0368 / 0.5 = 0.074, goats 0.0368 / 0.45 = 0.082 (the cow's yield applied to the small ruminants by analogy; a modern slaughter cow is fatter than a traditional animal). Complaint 532 pass: kids a kidding 1.62 for Landim goats (McKinnon and Rocha Table 1, fao.org/4/x5464b/x5464b0w.htm, opened) replaces the assumed 1.1; breeding-doe share 0.365 is the sheep figure (see sheep_kg source) by analogy, a labelled heuristic (retire: Complaints/670). Horn: no goat or sheep horn weight was found in an opened source (a Nigerian goat hoof and horn paper was seen only in a search summary, with no unit); 0.05 kg is the cattle horn per kilogram of live weight (0.33 kg at 167.64 kg, Bangladesh, see cattle_kg source) scaled to a 25 kg goat, was 0.1 (no source). Herder charge: Varro 2.3.10 (LacusCurtius, opened): goat flocks of about fifty are 'large enough' and in the Sallentine and Casinum districts 'about a hundred' are grazed together; one goatherd to a flock of 100 (was 150, no source). Doe share 0.365 is bracketed above by the female share of pastoral goat herds, 72 to 74 percent (FAO, Cattle and small ruminant production systems in sub-Saharan Africa, Table 11, https://www.fao.org/4/y4176e/y4176e06.htm, opened). Bran 4 kg a head-year: bracket only, 0 for an unsupplemented control to 68 to 200 g a day in trials on Ethiopian goats (search summary, not opened), so not cited as a figure.
goat_kg.basis: Live weight of goats of an unimproved breed. Increase = 0.365 of the herd breeding does (the sheep row's breeding-female share, Wollo highland flocks, used by analogy: no goat herd structure was found) x 0.919 kidding x 1.62 kids a kidding (Landim goats, McKinnon and Rocha Table 1) x 0.8 surviving to eight months = 0.435. Loss 0.08 adult mortality (assumed). Breeding group a buck and four does of about 25 kg, 125 kg (TEMPORARY HEURISTIC). Herd parameters for data/production/95_herds.json: 2 head per hectare of browse (no source found), 25 kg mean live weight at slaughter, half the herd milked for 51.12 kg a lactation (284 g a day for 180 days, Wilson; 25.56 kg a head-year), fat 5 percent of a lean carcass, skin 11 percent of live weight, 0.05 kg of horn a head (cattle horn per kilogram of live weight, 0.33 kg / 167.64 kg, scaled to 25 kg), 3 kg of salt a head-year. Offtake 0.214 is below natural increase less loss (0.405).

cattle_kg.dung_and_fodder_source: Dung and fodder per head, by the species row. Fresh excreta as a share of live weight a day: USDA NRCS, Agricultural Waste Management Field Handbook, Part 651, chapter 4 'Agricultural Waste Characteristics' (rev. July 1996; opened as a PDF): Table 4-18, lamb waste as excreted, weight 40.00 lb/d/1000#, so 0.04 for sheep; Table 4-8, beef waste as excreted, cow 63.00 lb/d/1000# (feeder yearlings 51.20 to 59.10), so 0.063 for cattle. The chapter has no goat row: goats use the sheep figure (no source found for goats; TEMPORARY HEURISTIC). Collected share is the part of the day in a fold, byre or night corral, a third (assumed): dung dropped at pasture is not gathered. Winter ration: dry matter intake of two percent of live weight a day (South Australian government fact sheet 'Calculating dry matter intakes for various classes of stock', Managing livestock in dry times, opened as a PDF: 'Animal on dry pasture or poor quality feed: 2%'; 'Cattle and sheep generally consume between 2-3% of their live weight in DM daily') over ninety days of stall or fold feeding (assumed), half of it straw at ninety percent dry matter (assumed). Bran is a supplement for milked animals (assumed). Confidence D: the excreta share and the dry matter intake are read (above); the collected share, winter days and straw share are assumed. Husbandry assumptions, searched in the same pass: the dung collected from an animal is the share of its day spent in the fold or byre (an extension worksheet, Keeping Track of Manure Nutrients in Dairy Pastures, https://www.kpu.ca/sites/default/files/Keeping%20Track%20of%20Manure%20Nutrients%20in%20Dairy%20Pastures.pdf, opened: a cow grazed 9 hours by day and 9 by night 'deposits 75 percent of her daily waste production' in the field and the other 25 percent in the confinement facility), so the collected share of a third is 8 hours of 24 in a night fold, the same order as that example's 25 percent. Winter housing: a Romanian dairy study (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3674972, opened) has cows pasturing 182 days a year, so about half a year indoors in a continental climate; the 90 days of stall or fold feeding here are a milder Mediterranean-and-oceanic ballpark under that. No page gave a straw share of a winter ration or a draught share of offtake; those stay assumed. Straw share of the winter ration, read in the Complaint 670 pass: Saskatchewan Agriculture, Straw as a roughage source (saskatchewan.ca ... /cattle/straw-roughage-source, opened): a cow can eat 'maximum 1.25% of her body weight' of straw, and straw can be up to 75 percent of a wintering cow's diet with good-quality straw and roughly 50 percent with low-quality straw; the 0.5 here is the low-quality case for a traditional farm's straw. Draught share, read: about 9 to 10 million of 31 million Ethiopian cattle are used for draught, 29 to 32 percent of the herd (cgspace.cgiar.org/items/98d68dea-662c-4b13-a0fe-51913e85bc2e, opened), and 0.3 is that herd share, kept as the share of each year's offtake kept to work (a steady-state replacement of working oxen at their five-year life from a 10 percent offtake would be higher, 0.6; the herd share is the cited figure). Goat excreta: the average 25 kg goat in Mgeta, Tanzania 'leaves 61 kg Total Solids (TS) droppings per year' (library.au.int record of Msalya et al., opened), 0.167 kg dry a day, 0.67 percent of live weight; fresh goat manure is 56, 52 and 62 percent moisture (Ingold et al., Tropentag 2020 abstract 417, opened), mean dry matter 43 percent, so fresh droppings are 0.0067 / 0.43 = 1.6 percent of live weight a day, faeces only; the 4 percent kept is the sheep as-excreted figure, faeces and urine together, so 1.6 percent is the lower bound of the bracket (urine not measured for goats).
cattle_kg.source: FAO, 'Production parameters of ruminants in traditional systems' (chapter 5 of the FAO review of ruminant production in sub-Saharan Africa; fao.org/4/Y4176E/y4176e08.htm; undated, 1990s), the same source as dairy_cattle_kg: calving rate 58.7 percent, calf mortality 21.7 percent, adult cow mortality 6.3 percent, milk offtake about 250 kg per lactation (opened and quoted: 'The mean of reported offtake rates for cattle in traditional systems is 9.9 percent (median of 9 percent)'; 'The mean weight of mature cows in traditional systems is 244 kg (median of 250 kg)'; 'Milk offtake per lactation in traditional systems is generally low, at an average of 252 kg (median of 251 kg)'). Dressing (45 to 50 percent for zebu-type cattle), fat, hide and horn shares, salt lick (about 30 g a day) and stocking rate: no source found (the chapter does not give them); kept as labelled heuristics (Complaints/670). Draught share of offtake (the share of each year's offtake kept out of the slaughter, castrated and reared to work age at the same live weight): no source found; a labelled heuristic (retire: Complaints/670). A working ox lasts about five years in work (data/world/service_lives.json, Langdon via Medievalists.net). Dressing and hide, read in the Complaints/532 and 670 source pass: Mummed and Webb, 'Carcass weight, meat yield and meat cuts from Arado, Boran, Barka, Raya cattle breeds in Ethiopia', Journal of Agricultural Science 11(18), 45-51 (2019), abstract opened at repository.up.ac.za/handle/2263/74394: export-abattoir cattle (2011), average live weight, warm carcass weight, cold carcass weight and warm dressing percentage 241.41, 106.93, 101.19 kg and 44.21%; the row's 250 kg animal takes 0.442 (was 0.48, no source; a warm carcass, the cold one is 41.9 percent). FAO, 'Manual for the slaughter of small ruminants in developing countries' (Animal Production and Health Paper 49), section 10.2, fao.org/4/x6552e/x6552e10.htm, opened: the approximate yield of green hides and skins in pastoral tropical livestock, as a percentage of live weight: cattle 6 to 8 (average 18 kg), large sheep and goats 14 to 16 (6 kg), dwarf sheep and goats 10 to 12 (4 kg). The 7 percent hide share is the midpoint of the cattle range, now read. Salt and stocking: see the sheep row's source (Complaint 670 pass): 30 g of salt a day for a mature cow (Agriorbit) is the 11 kg; 0.5 head a hectare is 2 ha a tropical livestock unit (Sange et al., LRRD 2018). Fat share and draught share stay labelled heuristics (a fed steer's fat trim is about 20 percent of the carcass in a South Dakota State University extension example found by search and not opened, which is not a lean traditional animal). Fat share, read in the Complaint 670 pass: USDA AMS By-Product Drop Value Report - Cow (https://www.ams.usda.gov/mnreports/ams_2834.pdf, opened as a PDF): renderable tallow yield 3.68 lb per 100 lb live weight of a typical slaughter cow, 3.68 percent of live weight; fat share of the carcass is that over the dressing fraction: cattle 0.0368 / 0.442 = 0.083, sheep 0.0368 / 0.5 = 0.074, goats 0.0368 / 0.45 = 0.082 (the cow's yield applied to the small ruminants by analogy; a modern slaughter cow is fatter than a traditional animal). Complaint 532 pass, horn: Bangladesh slaughterhouse by-product study of indigenous cattle (https://banglajol.info/index.php/BJAS/article/view/15784/11188, opened as a PDF): average live weight 167.64 kg and horn 0.33 +/- 0.04 kg an animal (by age class 0.20 to 0.72 kg); scaled to the row's 250 kg animal 0.33 x 250 / 167.64 = 0.49 kg, so 0.5 stands (the study's 'horn' may include the bony core, so the sheath alone is somewhat lighter). The same study's hide is 14.02 kg, 8.4 percent of live weight, near the row's 7 percent (FAO 6 to 8). Complaint 532 pass 4, herder charge 80 head: bracket, wide. Settled low end: the average Borana family keeps eight cows, cows being 45 percent of the herd, so about 18 head to a household's herders (FAO, Borana section, https://www.fao.org/4/x5461e/x5461e0r.htm, opened). Trail high end: Wikipedia, Cowboy (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cowboy, opened): an average drive herd of about 3,000 head and a crew of at least 10 cowboys, about 300 head a man on the move (own division). 80 lies between, near the geometric mean of 18 and 300 (73). Milking 0.1 hour a cow: hand milking took 11.91 minutes a cow for Holstein and Jersey crosses giving 7.58 kg a day at 0.32 kg a minute (Nepal field trial, https://cigrjournal.org/index.php/Ejounral/article/download/6949/3733/35161, opened as a PDF); a traditional cow giving 250 kg over 210 days gives 0.6 kg a milking, 1.9 minutes at that flow rate, so 6 minutes (0.1 hour) with preparation lies between 1.9 and 11.9 minutes. Slaughter, flaying and jointing 8 hours a carcass: see pig_kg and sheep_kg (a first-time home butcher takes 3 to 4 hours for an animal of 100 to 300 lb); a 250 kg steer is about twice the top of that range, so 7 to 8 hours is the same pace.
cattle_kg.basis: Live weight of unselected cattle, in kilograms. Rates are dairy_cattle_kg's (half the herd breeding cows x 0.587 calving x (1 - 0.217) calf survival; adult loss 0.063). Milk per head-year is half the herd x 0.587 calvings x 250 kg a lactation = 73.375 kg. Herd parameters for data/production/95_herds.json: 0.5 head per hectare of extensive grazing, 250 kg live weight at slaughter, dressing 0.442 (Mummed and Webb 2019), rendered fat 6 percent of the carcass, green hide 7 percent of live weight (FAO 6 to 8), 0.5 kg of horn sheaths a slaughtered animal, 11 kg of salt a head-year. Offtake 0.10 is below natural increase less loss (0.167). Oxen come out of the same herd: draught_share_of_offtake of the year's offtake is kept to work (Complaints/532); mules and horses are still draught_animal_kg's own recipe.

turkey_kg.source: Wikipedia, Wild turkey (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wild_turkey, opened): 'An adult male (tom or gobbler) normally weighs from 5 to 11 kg', 'the average weight of adult males is 7.6 kg', 'The adult female (hen) is typically much smaller at 2.5-5.4 kg', 'the average weight of adult females is 4.26 kg', 'Hens lay a clutch of 10-14 eggs, usually one per day'. Speller et al. 2018, Diversity of management strategies in Mesoamerican turkeys (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5792941/, opened): in the Postclassic 'turkeys were relying ever more heavily on provisioned maize or other C4 plants', and 'the number of turkey bones in archaeological sites overtakes those of leporids, dogs or white-tailed deer' in the Middle/Late Postclassic (1250-1521 CE). It gives no body weight, egg, flock or offtake figure. Nothing else was read; LABELLED HEURISTIC, conf D, no source found for the increase and loss rates, the breeding group, dressing percentage, fat and feather shares, maize ration and keeper ratio.
turkey_kg.basis: Live weight of the domestic turkey, kilograms. 5.93 kg is the mean of the opened wild-turkey averages for a tom (7.6 kg) and a hen (4.26 kg), an even sex ratio at slaughter assumed (the Mesoamerican domestic bird's own weight was not found). Increase 1.6 a head: a hen lays one clutch of 12 (middle of the opened 10-14), half the flock are hens, and about a third of eggs reach slaughter age, which is 2 young a bird before losses; 1.6 allows for that being optimistic. TEMPORARY HEURISTIC, retire: Complaints/654 follow-up (a zooarchaeological flock reconstruction). Loss 0.15 and a breeding group of 18 birds (about one tom to five hens, 5.93 kg each is 107 kg, rounded) are estimates of the same kind. Offtake 1.0 a head-year is below increase less loss (1.45). The birds are fed maize (opened: Postclassic isotopes show provisioned maize), 25 kg a head-year, no source found for the quantity. No pasture: a yard bird, so no land entry and no grows_on.

dog_kg.source: A museum note (https://www.monah.org/artifact-blog/2020/8/21/colima-dogs, opened) cites Sahagun, Florentine Codex 9:48 (Sahagun 1950-1982; the Codex itself not opened): dogs were 'bought ... to provide the people as food'. The note gives no weight, litter or offtake figure. No Mesoamerican dog body mass was found (a search summary gave only a Pathe-site dog about 40.5 cm high, a height, not a weight, and not opened). Nothing else was read; LABELLED HEURISTIC, conf D, no source found for live weight, increase, loss, breeding group, dressing, fat and hide shares, ration and keeper ratio.
dog_kg.basis: Live weight of the small Mesoamerican dog, 10 kg: TEMPORARY HEURISTIC, retire: Complaints/654 follow-up (a zooarchaeological body-mass estimate), no source found. Increase 1.2 and loss 0.15 a head are estimates of the same kind (a bitch rearing a couple of pups a year, half the pack bitches); offtake 0.5 is below increase less loss (1.05). A breeding group of 30 kg is three animals. Fed household maize scraps, 60 kg a head-year (no source found). No pasture: a household animal.

pig_kg.dung_and_fodder_source: Dung and fodder per head, as the sheep row (sheep_kg 'dung_and_fodder_source' in this file); no swine row was opened in the NRCS handbook, so the sheep excreta share is borrowed (TEMPORARY HEURISTIC, retire: Complaints/670). Bran: pigs are fed grain offal as well as forage; 60 kg a head-year is an assumed ration (no source found).
pig_kg.source: Varro, De re rustica 2.4 (LacusCurtius, opened through a page fetch, first 100000 characters): the sow 'bears twice a year' (2.4.14), a sow 'can feed eight little pigs at first' (2.4.19), young stay with the dam about two months (2.4.13), a barrow is cut at six months to a year (2.4.21), 'ten boars are enough for 100 sows' (2.4.22). Oyieng, Marshall and Gauly, 'Production parameters estimates of smallholder pig production systems in Uganda' (Tropentag 2023 abstract, https://www.tropentag.de/2023/abstracts/links/Oyieng_Vhqfvk7g.php, opened): litter size 7.2, piglets weaned per sow per year 7.1, farrowing interval 261 days (a modern Ugandan smallholder survey, not a Roman figure). Live weight, dressing, lard share, hide share, stocking rate, salt lick, breeding-sow share, mortality, grain ration and dung: no source found; labelled heuristics (retire: Complaints/670). Bristle: yield per slaughtered pig has no source found (a search turned up only an Indian study of pig hair fibre per clipping of live animals, 1.65 to 33.2 g, seen in a search summary and not opened); 0.2 kg is a labelled heuristic (retire: Complaints/670). The sorting labour, 0.5 hour a kilogram, is the figure of the former stand-alone bristles_kg entry (conf C, no source recorded there). Complaint 532 pass: dressing 0.70: The Livestock Conservancy, Heritage Swine Guide, Meat Processing (https://livestockconservancy.org/heritage-swine/heritage-swine-guide/meat-processing/, opened): 'The average pork carcass dressing percentage will be around 70% of the live weight'; University of Maine Extension Bulletin 1073 (https://extension.umaine.edu/publications/1073e/, opened): 'Heritage breed dressing percentages vary from 64-75%' (was 0.75, no source) and 'the skin is approximately 6%' of liveweight (was 0.04, no source). Live weight: Livestock Conservancy, American Guinea Hog (https://livestockconservancy.org/heritage-breeds/heritage-breeds-list/american-guinea-hog/, opened): boars 175 to 200 lb, sows 85 to 150 lb (79 to 91 kg and 39 to 68 kg); the same Conservancy table gives hot carcass weights from 140 lb (Guinea) to 252 lb (Hereford); 60 kg is a mixed herd of sows and growers, a bracket and not a measurement. Litter, bracketing the sow increase: Mangalica (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mangalica, opened): slightly over 7,000 sows producing around 60,000 piglets a year, about 8.6 a sow-year; Guinea hog litters 6 to 10 twice a year (Conservancy page). Lard share: USDA AMS By-Product Drop Value Report - Hogs NW_LS446 (http://www.ams.usda.gov/mnreports/ams_2835.pdf, opened as a PDF; report for 2 to 6 Nov 2026): a typical 280 lb slaughter hog at 74 percent dressing gives 1.72 lb lard and 0.50 lb choice white grease a hundredweight live, so 2.22 / 74 = 3.0 percent of a modern lean carcass; the American Guinea Hog's saleable yield is 66 percent of the hot carcass and its lean muscle 24 percent (SARE/Livestock Conservancy, Heritage Hog Carcass Yields, https://projects.sare.org/wp-content/uploads/1023Heritage_Hog_Carcass_Yields.pdf, opened as a PDF), so the fat, bone and skin of a lard-type carcass are up to 34 percent. The row's 0.3 lies in that bracket (3 to 34 percent) near its top; no opened figure fixes it, so it stays a labelled heuristic. Salt: pig rations need 0.25 percent salt for growers and 0.5 percent for breeding stock (Family Farm Livestock, https://familyfarmlivestock.com/pigs-and-salt-do-they-really-need-it/, opened); feed intake about 2.5 kg a day near finishing weights (AHDB, https://ahdb.org.uk/knowledge-library/feeding-growing-and-finishing-pigs, opened: 0.5 kg a day at 13 kg 'up to 2.5 kg/day or more' at 110 kg); salt 0.85 x 0.0025 x 2.5 x 365 + 0.15 x 0.005 x 2.5 x 365 = 2.6 kg a head-year (was 6, no source). Stocking, bracket only: 0.16 to 0.4 pigs an acre (0.4 to 1.0 a hectare) for acorn fattening of 42 to 100 days (UC ANR, Pastured Pig Production in California Oak Woodlands, https://ccfruitandnuts.ucanr.edu/sites/default/files/2020-10/338269.pdf, opened as a PDF); 2 a hectare year-round on woodland and fallow is above that and far below rotated pasture; it stays a labelled heuristic. Figure confidences from the Complaint 532 coordinator pass (a cited bracket that holds the value counts): lard share 0.3 of carcass, C, bracket 3 to 34 percent above; sow share 0.15, C, derived: Varro 2.4.22 ten boars to 100 sows and 2.4.21 barrows cut at six months to a year, so growers on hand a sow are 7.1 weaned x about 0.75 year = 5.3, and sows are 1 / (1 + 0.1 + 5.3) = 0.156 of the herd; stocking 2 a hectare, C only as a bracket (0.4 to 1.0 a hectare acorn fattening to rotated pasture, which is far higher), loose; bran 60 kg a head-year, bracket 0 to 2.5 kg a day total feed of which up to half may be forage (AHDB; Family Farm Livestock), loose. Complaint 532 pass 4, herder charge 100 head: Varro 2.4.22 (LacusCurtius, opened): 'sed ego modicum puto centenarium' (a herd of a hundred is moderate), some keep up to 150, and a smaller herd 'quod comites subulcus pauciores quaerit' (needs fewer swineherd companions), so a swineherd with companions takes a herd of about a hundred; the Domesday book counts woodland by pigs (Hampstead woodland for 100 pigs), no pigs per swineherd. Loss 0.1: bracket, post-weaning mortality of smallholder pigs 1 to 5 percent and adults under 2 percent as targets (search summary only, not opened), so the 0.1 is not bounded and stays a heuristic. Slaughter 3 hours a carcass: a pig took 90 minutes from drop to hung quarters and 9 hours stun to packaged (permies thread above), about 4 hours a pig for two people (Grit above).
pig_kg.basis: Live weight of unimproved pigs, in kilograms. Increase = 0.15 of the herd breeding sows (assumed; Varro's ten boars to 100 sows only fixes the boars) x 7.1 weaned piglets a sow-year (Uganda smallholder survey above) = 1.065 head a head-year. Loss 0.1 (assumed). Offtake 0.8 is below natural increase less loss (0.965): pigs are fattened and slaughtered within the year. A breeding group is a boar and three sows, 300 kg of about 75 kg (TEMPORARY HEURISTIC). Herd parameters beside it feed the herd recipe lard_kg in data/production/95_herds.json: 2 head per hectare of woodland and fallow grazing, 60 kg live weight at slaughter (inside the 39 to 91 kg adult American Guinea Hog range), dressing 0.70 of live weight, 0.3 of the carcass rendered as lard (a labelled heuristic, bracketed in the source), a raw skin 6 percent of live weight, 2.6 kg of salt a head-year (0.85 x 0.0025 x 2.5 kg feed a day x 365 + 0.15 x 0.005 x 2.5 x 365). Bristle is a joint product of the slaughter (bristles_kg): the household brush node takes it as a research material (data/branches/12_household.json).

horse_kg.dung_and_fodder_source: Dung and fodder per head as the cattle row (cattle_kg 'dung_and_fodder_source' in this file); no equine row was opened in the NRCS handbook, so the cattle excreta share is borrowed (TEMPORARY HEURISTIC, retire: Complaints/670). Bran is an assumed grain ration for working animals (no source found).
horse_kg.source: Varro, De re rustica 2.7 and 2.8 (LacusCurtius, opened through a page fetch, first 100000 characters): horse breeding stock not under three nor over ten years old and 'one [stallion] to every ten mares' (2.7.1); mating from the vernal equinox to the solstice (2.7.7); 'those who mate their mares every other year claim that they breed for a longer time', annual breeding wears mares out sooner (2.7.11); foals kept with the dam two years (2.7.12); breaking at three years old (2.7.13); 'the mule is the offspring of a mare and an ass', 'neither brings any return from young' (2.8.2); a jack is used for breeding after three years (2.8.2). Foaling rate and mortality of a working-horse population were looked for: the one survey opened (Sowe, Gai, Sumberg and Gilbert, 'Foaling and mortality of equines in The Gambia: a national survey', FAO, fao.org/4/x5455b/x5455b1d.htm, survey of December 1987) reports foaling 24 percent for horses and mortality 27 percent for both equines in a tsetse-affected country; it is not used, since the trypanosomiasis loss of a place is taken from data/disease/endemic and not from the row. Live weight, stocking rate, hide share, salt, bran, the herder's charge and the breaking hours: no source found; labelled heuristics (retire: Complaints/670). Complaint 532 pass: live weight: Wikipedia, Fjord horse (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fjord_horse, opened): 'The weight normally ranges from 400 to 500 kilograms'; Nordgen, Icelandic horse (https://www.nordgen.org/our-work/farm-animals/nordic-native-breeds/icelandic-horse, opened): 350-400 kg; 400 kg is the traditional-breed range, so it stands. Stocking: University of Arkansas Extension FSA3165 (https://www.uaex.uada.edu/publications/PDF/FSA3165.pdf, opened as a PDF): a horse needs 3 to 5 acres on pasture growing 2 to 4 tons an acre, so 0.5 to 0.83 a hectare; 0.5 stands. Salt: Equus magazine (https://equusmagazine.com/horse-care/eqsalt203/, opened): the NRC suggests horses at rest need 25 g of sodium chloride a day (9.1 kg a year) and horses in light to moderate work 55 to 65 g (20 to 24 kg); 11 kg (30 g a day) is a herd mostly at rest or not yet in work. Foaling and foal survival, bracketing the 0.5 foals a mare-year and 0.8 survival: Assateague ponies, Keiper and Houpt 1984 (https://madbarn.com/research/reproduction-in-feral-horses-an-eight-year-study, abstract opened): foaling rate 57.1 percent, foal survival 88.3 percent; Pryor Mountain wild horses 1993-2007 (https://www.usgs.gov/publications/demography-pryor-mountain-wild-horses-1993-2007, opened): foaling 0.576 a mare of three or older, annual foal survival 0.697. Both are free-living herds mated every year, not Varro's alternate-year mares. The mare share of the herd (0.35), bran and the herder's charge still have no source. Herder charge: Varro 2.10.11 (LacusCurtius, opened, Latin): 'ad equarum gregem quinquagenarium bini homines', two men to a herd of fifty mares, so 25 mares a man; with 0.435 of the head mares that is 25 / 0.435 = 57 head a herder (was 100, no source). Bran 40 kg a head-year: bracketed from 0 (light work is kept on hay alone, ration 1 of Table 3) to 2 to 3 kg a day of oats for a 500 kg horse in moderate work (Alberta Agriculture, Feeding working and performance horses, agdex 460/50-1, www1.agriculture.alberta.ca, opened as a PDF; Tables 3 and 4); the herd's animals are not in work, so the low end is the relevant one. Mare share and increase: derived above from Varro 2.7.1, 2.7.11-13. Complaint 532 pass 4, breaking to harness 60 hours a head: Horse Illustrated, Horse training: the first three months (http://www.horseillustrated.com/horse-training-first-three-months, opened): 15 to 20 hours of groundwork in weeks 1 to 3, 10 to 15 hours in weeks 4 and 5 and 5 hours in week 6 (30 to 40 hours before the first ride), then hour-long sessions through weeks 7 to 12; six weeks of those at three to five sessions a week is 18 to 30 hours, so 48 to 70 hours; 60 is inside. Adult loss 0.07: Pryor Mountain pooled annual survival 0.899 across ages and sexes, so mortality 0.10 pooled (source above).
horse_kg.basis: Live weight of breeding and working horses, in kilograms. Increase 0.174 = breeding mares 0.435 of the head x 0.5 foals a mare-year (mares mated every other year, Varro 2.7.11) x 0.8 foals surviving (inside the 0.70 to 0.88 first-year survival of the Pryor Mountain and Assateague herds, see source). Mare share = 1 / (1 + 0.1 stallions a mare, Varro 2.7.1 + 3 years of young kept before breaking, Varro 2.7.12-13, x 0.5 foals x 0.8 survival = 1.2 young) = 0.435. Loss 0.07 (assumed). Offtake 0.06 is the head reared to work (Varro 2.7.13: broken at three) and leaving the herd for harness, below increase less loss (0.07). A breeding group is a stallion and ten mares at 400 kg (Varro 2.7.1 for the ratio, the weight assumed). Dead animals are skinned; their flesh is not eaten here (a labelled choice: no equine meat in the food goods). Herder: 57 head. Parameters beside it feed the herd recipe draught_animal_kg in data/production/95_herds.json.

mule_kg.dung_and_fodder_source: Dung and fodder per head as the cattle row (cattle_kg 'dung_and_fodder_source' in this file); no equine row was opened in the NRCS handbook, so the cattle excreta share is borrowed (TEMPORARY HEURISTIC, retire: Complaints/670). Bran is an assumed grain ration for working animals (no source found).
mule_kg.source: Varro, De re rustica 2.7 and 2.8 (LacusCurtius, opened through a page fetch, first 100000 characters): horse breeding stock not under three nor over ten years old and 'one [stallion] to every ten mares' (2.7.1); mating from the vernal equinox to the solstice (2.7.7); 'those who mate their mares every other year claim that they breed for a longer time', annual breeding wears mares out sooner (2.7.11); foals kept with the dam two years (2.7.12); breaking at three years old (2.7.13); 'the mule is the offspring of a mare and an ass', 'neither brings any return from young' (2.8.2); a jack is used for breeding after three years (2.8.2). Foaling in jennies: Deng, Shi, Li, Tang, Liao and Xie, 'A Cross-Sectional Survey of Foaling-Related Parameters of Jennies (Equus asinus) Under Smallholder Farm Conditions in Northeast China', Journal of Equine Veterinary Science 87 (2020) 102928 (abstract opened): overall foaling rate 75 percent and foaling interval 500.5 days in jennies, 2014 to 2017; it is a donkey dam, not a mare, so it brackets the alternate-year mating of Varro and is not used as the mare figure. A study of mule pregnancies in mares (foaling rate 71.9 percent, pregnancy loss 36.8 percent) came up in a search summary only and was not opened. Mule live weight, rearing survival, stud replacement, stocking rate and the rest: no source found; labelled heuristics (retire: Complaints/670). Complaint 532 pass: mule weight: Wikipedia, Mule (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mule, opened): 'The median weight range is between about 370 and 460 kg', so 415 kg replaces the assumed 350. Foaling of mares covered by jacks, bracketing the 0.5 foals a mare-year: Rossi et al. 2016 as quoted in a Brazilian paper (https://scielo.br/j/abmvz/a/PkYTvGw4zFgPr6tQ7Vz7KWg/?lang=en, opened): mule pregnancies foaling rate 64.08 percent, pregnancy loss 31.69 percent; Jordao, Camargo and Gouveia 1954 (Boletim da Industria Animal 14, 49-62, cited on that page): foaling rate 35.9 percent for mares bred naturally to jacks on pasture over 14 seasons. The 0.5 is inside 0.36 to 0.64; the 0.8 survival to work age, the 0.9 mare share and the herd salt, stocking and bran are those of horse_kg (above) or have no source. Herder charge: Varro 2.10.11 (see horse_kg): 25 mares a man; with mares 0.91 of the stud, 25 / 0.91 = 27 head a herder (was 100, no source). Bran: as horse_kg. Breaking to harness: as horse_kg.
mule_kg.basis: Live weight of the mule-breeding stud, in kilograms: mares and the jack asses that cover them (a mule is a mare by an ass, Varro 2.8.2; a mule does not breed). Offtake 0.36 is mules reared to work per stud head a year = mares 0.91 of the stud (a jack to ten mares, 10/11, Varro 2.7.1 applied to jacks) x 0.5 foals a mare-year (alternate-year mating, Varro 2.7.11) x 0.8 surviving to work age (inside the 0.70 to 0.88 first-year foal survival of the Pryor Mountain and Assateague herds; a lower bound on survival to three years, see source); each weighs mule_live_weight_kg_per_head (415 kg, the midpoint of the 370 to 460 kg median weight range, Wikipedia Mule). The stud itself is kept up by raising or buying replacement mares and jacks: increase 0.14 is that replacement: Varro 2.7.1 breeds stock 'not under three nor over ten' years, a working life of 7 years, so one seventh of the stud is replaced a year (loss 0.07, assumed). A breeding group is a jack and ten mares, 4400 kg. Parameters beside it feed the herd recipe draught_mule_kg in data/production/95_herds.json.
